responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character35_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Sure, I’ll speak as Character35_F.

Fairness, for me, isn't just about everyone getting the same thing—it's about everyone getting what they need, especially when some people start out with less. Growing up in a lower-class family, I saw first-hand how much harder it was for people who didn’t have connections or money. Fairness means more than just rules; it’s about making sure people aren’t left behind just because of where they’re from or what they look like.

Belonging is a big deal. There were times I felt out of place—like going to community events and sensing that people saw me differently because of my clothes or because my family didn’t have much. What made me feel like I belonged was when people reached out, remembered my name, treated me like I mattered even if I couldn’t contribute much. So, I think belonging is built by people making an effort to include everyone, especially the ones who feel invisible.

Community, to me, is about people looking out for each other. It’s not just living in the same place—it’s sharing worries, celebrating little things, sometimes arguing but coming together when someone needs help. My experience was that the people who didn’t judge, who were willing to listen and lend a hand, were the ones who made the community feel real. It’s about being connected despite differences, and caring about what happens to each other. I wish more people could feel that, no matter where they’re from or what their background is.

Those are the things I felt strongly about, based on what I lived.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character35_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting in the community garden and taking it all in, honestly, I’d feel a mix of things. Mostly, I’d feel curious and kind of hopeful, but also sometimes a little awkward or unsure—just being real.

I grew up around people who mostly looked like me and had similar backgrounds. So, seeing neighbors who speak different languages, dress differently, or have other ways of doing things—it stands out. But I don’t think that’s bad. I actually like hearing new stories and sometimes learning about other people’s food or family traditions. It makes the neighborhood less boring, you know?

At the same time, I can’t pretend it’s always easy. Sometimes I worry about saying the wrong thing or making someone uncomfortable if I mess up, or not understanding where someone is coming from. But I believe it’s important to try. If someone’s dealing with stuff like addiction or illness, I think it’s about being patient and not judging right away. Same for people in different kinds of relationships or with lifestyles I might not totally get.

Mostly, I just try to treat people the way I want to be treated—friendly, open, not making assumptions. If we all minded our own business but still pitched in when somebody needed help, I think it’d work out. What matters most is making space for everyone to be themselves, as long as there’s respect both ways. That’s how trust builds—just showing up, saying hi, and not acting like you’re above anyone.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
I think to make everyone feel comfortable, the main thing is respect and not jumping to conclusions. People really need to feel like they aren’t being judged just for how they live or what struggles they’ve got going on. I know from my own experience—growing up lower class—how easy it is for people to make assumptions, and how much it hurts when you feel looked down on. So I always try to keep that in mind.

If a neighbor’s dealing with alcoholism or substance abuse, I’d say what helps is not shaming them or gossiping. You don’t have to pretend nothing’s wrong, but you show kindness and offer help if they ask. Everyone’s got something, and just because their problems show more on the outside doesn’t mean they deserve less respect. I also think people with health issues—like infectious diseases—shouldn’t be treated like they’re dangerous. If there’s something people need to know to stay safe, it’s better to talk about it honestly instead of letting fear take over.

When it comes to differences in race, religion, language, or sexual orientation, I think even more communication and tolerance are needed. Sometimes people just don’t understand each other, and it can lead to awkwardness or even fights. If someone’s family looks different than what you grew up with, or if they celebrate holidays you’ve never heard of, it’s easy to feel out of place. That’s when it helps to ask questions, listen, and not make jokes or comments just because something feels unfamiliar. It’s better to admit you don’t know much and be open to learning.

I’m always willing to talk about why this matters. For me, it comes down to wanting a neighborhood where nobody feels scared to leave their house or ashamed of who they are. You don’t have to be best friends with everyone, but you should be able to say hello and know that you’re safe and respected. More communication breaks down walls—people stop seeing each other as “us and them.” Tolerance isn’t about ignoring differences; it’s about accepting them and focusing on what we have in common. That’s how you build real community, and I think we all need more of it.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character35_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s a tough one, and I’ve thought about it a lot, especially since jobs have always been a struggle where I’m from. When there aren’t enough jobs to go around, fairness means making sure the people who live here, who’ve been part of the community, have a real shot at work and a decent life. I get why folks worry when they see new people coming in and competing for the same jobs, especially low-wage ones, because for a lot of us, those are the only jobs we can get.

But at the same time, I don’t think it’s fair to blame immigrants for everything. A lot of them are just trying to survive, same as us. And sometimes, they take on jobs that others really don’t want, or fill gaps in the workforce that help keep things running. I think it’s about the system and not the individuals. Companies sometimes hire migrants because they can pay them less or get away with worse conditions—that’s wrong, and it hurts everybody.

So for balance, I’d say there should be rules to protect all workers, local or migrant—like making sure everyone gets at least minimum wage and safe conditions, and that companies can’t just pick the cheapest worker and treat people badly. Maybe there could be limits on how many people come in for certain types of work, especially when unemployment is high. But there should also be programs to help locals get skills or training for better jobs, so we’re not all fighting over scraps.

Fairness means not leaving anyone out, but it also means not ignoring the real struggles that people who already live here face. It’s about finding a way for everyone to have dignity and opportunity, instead of making us fight each other for survival. The government and employers should take responsibility, not just pit people against each other.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character35_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Looking at it from a national view, I think a lot of these arguments make sense in their own way—like, it’s complicated and not just black and white.

On the positive side, I do see that immigrants can fill jobs that really need doing, especially ones people locally aren’t lining up for. I’ve seen it myself—stuff like farm work, cleaning, care jobs, restaurant work. Without immigrants, some stuff just wouldn’t get done, or prices would go way up. And I’ll admit, the cultural side is real too. Having people from different backgrounds makes life more interesting, and you learn a lot—food, music, all sorts of things.

But I also get why people worry. If you’re someone who’s struggling to find work, it’s easy to feel like immigrants are competition, especially when you see companies hiring them for less. That can drive wages down for everyone, and make it harder for regular folks—especially those already on the edge. Those fears aren’t made up, but I think it’s more about employers trying to get cheap labor than about immigrants themselves.

About security and crime, I feel like that gets blown out of proportion sometimes. Yeah, there’s always a risk, but most people coming here just want a better life and aren’t trying to cause trouble. The media or politicians can stir up fear, and it’s hard to know what’s really true. I’d want to see actual numbers and facts before I judged, not just scary stories.

On the humanitarian side, I think it matters a lot. If someone’s running from war or persecution, we should help if we can. That’s just being human. But I also know there are limits—America can’t fix everything for everyone, and sometimes you have to make tough choices when there’s not enough to go around.

So, I find the jobs and culture arguments reasonable, and the worries about competition are real too. But stuff about crime or terrorism needs real evidence and shouldn’t be used to paint everyone as a threat. There’s room for more honest conversation and less fear-mongering. I think most people just want things to be fair and safe, and that’s not crazy. We need more facts and less hype, and definitely more listening to people’s real stories, not just headlines.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character35_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
If I had to pick, I wouldn’t go for complete openness or for refusing everyone—that just wouldn’t work. I guess I’d favour a mix of admitting people based on job demand and setting some limits, with exceptions for real humanitarian cases.

Letting anyone in, no matter what, sounds fair in theory, but in real life, with jobs and housing already tight, it could make things harder for people already struggling. You have to think about the folks living here who’ve always had to fight for stability. At the same time, just shutting the door on everyone else feels wrong and kind of heartless, especially for people who really need a safe place.

Admitting people based on job demand makes sense, but only if it’s done honestly—like, making sure companies aren’t just using it as an excuse to hire cheap workers and ignore local folks. It should be about filling real gaps, not just saving money for business. Setting reasonable numerical limits helps keep things from getting overwhelming, so services and communities aren’t stretched too thin.

But even with limits, I think there should be special rules for refugees or people in serious need. If someone’s running from war or persecution, we should find a way to help, even if it’s harder. That’s just being decent.

For social integration, it’d help if there were programs for both immigrants and locals—like language classes, job training, community events that actually bring people together, not just leave new arrivals on their own. Fairness isn’t just about who gets in; it’s about making sure everyone who’s here gets treated with respect and has a chance to be part of things.

So yeah, a balanced policy for me would be job-based admission with real limits, plus protection for refugees, and real support for integration. That way nobody’s left out, and the community can actually work together.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character35_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character35_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Thank you for asking. Stepping into Character35_F’s shoes like this, I realized just how much her views were shaped by real, everyday struggles—feeling left out, wanting things to be fair, and seeing how the system sometimes pits people against each other. It made me appreciate how practical and grounded her thinking was; she didn’t look at these issues just as ideas, but from how they actually affect people’s daily lives.

What stood out was how much empathy she had for both sides—locals worried about jobs and immigrants trying to survive. It wasn’t about blaming, but about looking for ways everyone could have dignity. I think I saw more clearly how important it is to balance compassion with reality, and not get stuck in extremes.

Honestly, it made me reflect on my own views too. I might have been quicker to defend open borders or humanitarian ideals before, but thinking as Character35_F reminded me that you also have to look out for the people who are already struggling. Policy isn’t just about what’s right in theory—it’s about what helps communities work in practice.

I feel more aware now of just how much background and experience shape our opinions, and why it’s important to listen to folks with different experiences. Character35_F’s perspective was about respecting everyone, finding real solutions, and never losing sight of fairness. I’m grateful for the chance to see things through her eyes, and I’ll carry that with me.
